points: **Cavernous sinus**: III, IV, V1, V2 in the lateral wall; ICA and VI lie within the sinus. V3 is NOT in the cavernous sinus (exits via foramen ovale)
Infection of the danger area of the face spreads via facial vein → superior ophthalmic vein/pterygoid plexus → cavernous sinus thrombosis (proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, V1/V2 sensory loss)
**Circle of Willis**: ICA, ACA, ACom, PCom, PCA (MCA is not part). Commonest berry aneurysm: ACom junction; PCom aneurysm → pupil-involving CN III palsy

**Internal capsule**: posterior limb (corticospinal) supplied by lenticulostriate branches of MCA + anterior choroidal artery (ICA); anterior limb also by recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA). Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriates → putaminal bleed

**Basal ganglia**: direct pathway (D1) facilitates movement, indirect (D2) inhibits; Parkinson = loss of substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons; hemiballismus = contralateral subthalamic nucleus; Huntington = caudate atrophy

**Cerebellum**: hemisphere lesions give IPSILATERAL limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, past-pointing; vermis → truncal ataxia (alcoholic anterior vermis degeneration). Sole output of cerebellar cortex = Purkinje cells (GABA, inhibitory) to deep nuclei
**Thalamic relays**: VPL (body somatosensory), VPM (face + taste), LGN (vision), MGN (hearing), VL (motor from cerebellum/basal ganglia), anterior nucleus (Papez circuit, via mammillothalamic tract)

**Rule of 4**: cranial nerve motor nuclei that divide 12 (III, IV, VI, XII) are medial; medial structures = Motor tract, Medial lemniscus, MLF; lateral = spinothalamic, sympathetic, spinocerebellar, spinal V

Nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI motor) lesion in lateral medulla → dysphagia, hoarseness; nucleus tractus solitarius = taste (VII, IX, X) + visceral afferents; facial colliculus = VI nucleus + looping VII fibres

traps.stem: Stab wound hemisects the cord on the RIGHT at T10. Where is pain and temperature lost?
traps.trap: Right side below T10 — tempting because every other deficit is ipsilateral
traps.fix: LEFT side from about T11–T12 down (spinothalamic fibres have already crossed). Right side: UMN paralysis + vibration/position loss; band of total anaesthesia at the level on the right

traps.stem: Earliest cranial nerve palsy in cavernous sinus thrombosis or an intracavernous ICA aneurysm?
traps.trap: Oculomotor (III) — it is the classic 'pupil' nerve and lies uppermost in the lateral wall
traps.fix: Abducens (VI): it runs free inside the sinus beside the ICA, unprotected by the dural wall, so lateral gaze palsy appears first

traps.stem: Vertigo, ipsilateral Horner, hoarseness, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain/temperature loss. Is there limb weakness?
traps.trap: Contralateral hemiparesis — confusing lateral with medial medullary syndrome
traps.fix: No weakness: lateral medullary (Wallenberg; vertebral artery > PICA) spares the pyramids. Medial medullary (anterior spinal artery/vertebral) = contralateral hemiparesis + contralateral DCML loss + ipsilateral tongue deviation (XII)

cards.front: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: which modalities are spared?
cards.back: Vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns, supplied by posterior spinal arteries). Motor and pain/temperature lost below the level.

cards.text: Spinothalamic fibres cross in the {{c1::anterior white commissure}} within 1–2 segments; dorsal column fibres cross in the {{c2::lower medulla (internal arcuate fibres)}}.

cards.front: Thalamic nucleus relaying taste and facial sensation?
cards.back: VPM (ventral posteromedial). VPL = body; LGN = vision; MGN = hearing.

cards.text: Hemiballismus results from a lesion of the {{c1::contralateral subthalamic nucleus}}.

cards.front: Side of signs in a cerebellar hemisphere lesion?
cards.back: Ipsilateral (double crossing of cerebellar outflow + corticospinal tract).

points: **Pouches**: 1st → middle ear, Eustachian tube, mastoid antrum; 2nd → palatine tonsil epithelium; 3rd → inferior parathyroid + thymus; 4th → superior parathyroid + ultimobranchial body. 1st cleft → external acoustic meatus; branchial cyst is usually a 2nd-cleft remnant at anterior border of SCM
Inferior parathyroid (3rd pouch) migrates further with the thymus → more often ectopic (e.g. mediastinal)

**Tongue**: anterior 2/3 — general sensation lingual (V3), taste chorda tympani (VII); posterior 1/3 incl. circumvallate papillae — IX (both); root/epiglottic region — internal laryngeal (X). All muscles XII except palatoglossus (X, pharyngeal plexus)
**Larynx**: cricothyroid (tensor) — external laryngeal nerve; all other intrinsic muscles — recurrent laryngeal. Sensation above cords internal laryngeal, below cords recurrent laryngeal

**Pterygopalatine fossa**: V2, pterygopalatine ganglion, 3rd part of maxillary artery; communicates with orbit (inferior orbital fissure), nasal cavity (sphenopalatine foramen), middle cranial fossa (foramen rotundum, pterygoid canal). Greater petrosal fibres relay here → lacrimal gland

**Parotid**: facial nerve divides within the gland (most superficial structure, superficial to retromandibular vein and ECA) into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical. Secretomotor: IX → tympanic → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal (Frey syndrome after parotidectomy)
**Scalp (SCALP)**: Skin, dense Connective tissue (vessels held open → profuse bleeding), Aponeurosis (galea), Loose areolar tissue (danger area: emissary veins → intracranial spread), Pericranium

**Neck triangles**: anterior = submental, submandibular, carotid, muscular; posterior = occipital + subclavian. Spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle → trapezius palsy after node biopsy. Carotid bifurcation at upper border of thyroid cartilage (C3–C4)
**Dangerous area of face** (upper lip, nose): facial vein ↔ superior ophthalmic vein & deep facial vein → pterygoid plexus → cavernous sinus thrombosis

traps.stem: Superior parathyroid glands develop from which pharyngeal pouch?
traps.trap: 3rd pouch — 'superior' sounds like it should come from the higher numbered pouch above
traps.fix: 4th pouch. The inferior parathyroids come from the 3rd pouch (with the thymus) and descend past the 4th-pouch glands

traps.stem: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve damage after thyroidectomy causes stridor. Which muscle's loss explains it?
traps.trap: Lateral cricoarytenoid or cricothyroid
traps.fix: Posterior cricoarytenoid — sole abductor. Cricothyroid (external laryngeal) is spared, so cords lie paramedian and airway narrows

traps.stem: Middle meningeal artery traverses which foramen?
traps.trap: Foramen ovale (it is right next door and carries the accessory meningeal artery)
traps.fix: Foramen spinosum. Ovale = V3, accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, emissary vein

cards.text: Stapes, styloid process and lesser horn of hyoid derive from the {{c1::2nd}} arch (Reichert's cartilage); malleus and incus from the {{c2::1st}} arch.

cards.front: Only muscle derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch?
cards.back: Stylopharyngeus (supplied by IX).

cards.front: Taste from the circumvallate papillae is carried by?
cards.back: Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) — though they lie just anterior to the sulcus terminalis.

cards.text: The only tongue muscle not supplied by XII is {{c1::palatoglossus}}, supplied by {{c2::vagus via the pharyngeal plexus}}.
Ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells) arises from the {{c1::4th}} pharyngeal pouch.

cards.front: Which scalp layer is the 'dangerous layer' and why?
cards.back: Loose areolar tissue (4th layer): emissary veins connect it to dural sinuses, so infection spreads intracranially.

verify: Langman's Embryology + BDC Vol 3. Laryngeal cartilages: Langman says 4th + 6th arches jointly; BDC tables thyroid → 4th, cricoid/arytenoid → 6th
algorithm:
Pharyngeal arches — nerve decides the structure
→ 1st arch (nerve V): muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly digastric, tensor tympani, tensor palati; malleus, incus; Meckel cartilage
→ 2nd arch (VII): muscles of facial expression, stapedius, posterior belly digastric, stylohyoid; stapes, styloid process, lesser horn + upper body hyoid
→ 3rd arch (IX): stylopharyngeus; greater horn + lower body hyoid
→ 4th arch (SLN, branch of X): cricothyroid, levator palati, pharyngeal constrictors; thyroid cartilage
→ 6th arch (RLN, branch of X): intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid; cricoid, arytenoid cartilages
Pouches: 1 = tympanic cavity + Eustachian tube | 2 = palatine tonsil | 3 dorsal = inferior parathyroid, 3 ventral = thymus | 4 = superior parathyroid | ultimobranchial body = C cells of thyroid
→ Failure of 3rd + 4th pouch → DiGeorge (22q11): hypocalcaemia + absent thymus

**Root values**: musculocutaneous C5–C7; axillary C5–C6; radial C5–T1; median C5/6–T1; ulnar C8–T1 (± C7)
**Dermatomes**: C5 lateral arm, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm; reflexes: biceps C5–6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7

**Rotator cuff (SITS)**: supraspinatus (initiates abduction 0–15°, most commonly torn/impinged), infraspinatus + teres minor (lateral rotation), subscapularis (medial rotation). Deltoid abducts 15–90°; trapezius + serratus anterior above 90°
**Axillary artery**: 3 parts by pectoralis minor — 1 branch (superior thoracic), 2 (thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic), 3 (subscapular, anterior & posterior circumflex humeral)

**Scapular anastomosis**: suprascapular + dorsal scapular (from subclavian) with circumflex scapular (from subscapular) — links 1st part subclavian to 3rd part axillary; keeps the limb perfused if the axillary artery is ligated between thyrocervical trunk and subscapular origin
**Elbow anastomosis**: superior/inferior ulnar collateral + profunda branches ↔ radial, ulnar and interosseous recurrent arteries
Supracondylar humerus fracture: brachial artery (Volkmann ischaemic contracture) + median/anterior interosseous nerve; medial epicondyle fracture: ulnar nerve

traps.stem: Which structure passes through the carpal tunnel?
traps.trap: Ulnar nerve or flexor carpi radialis/palmaris longus — all are close to the retinaculum
traps.fix: Median nerve + FPL + 4 FDS + 4 FDP. Ulnar nerve/artery run in Guyon's canal; palmaris longus is superficial to the retinaculum; FCR has its own split compartment

traps.stem: Ulnar nerve cut at the elbow vs at the wrist — which gives more marked clawing?
traps.trap: Elbow lesion, because it is 'higher' and more muscles are lost
traps.fix: Wrist lesion (ulnar paradox): at the elbow, ulnar half of FDP is also paralysed, so fingers do not flex at the IP joints and the claw is less obvious

traps.stem: Winging of scapula after axillary node clearance — nerve injured?
traps.trap: Thoracodorsal nerve (also in the axilla; supplies latissimus dorsi)
traps.fix: Long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) → serratus anterior. Thoracodorsal injury weakens extension/adduction but does not wing the scapula

points: **Gluteal injection**: upper outer (superolateral) quadrant or ventrogluteal site — avoids the sciatic nerve (exits below piriformis via greater sciatic foramen)

**Common peroneal** winds round the neck of fibula → foot drop, loss of eversion and dorsiflexion, sensory loss dorsum of foot; deep peroneal alone → first web space anaesthesia. Tibial → loss of plantar flexion and inversion

**Venous drainage**: great saphenous anterior to medial malleolus → saphenous opening → femoral vein (~3–4 cm inferolateral to pubic tubercle); small saphenous behind lateral malleolus → popliteal vein. Perforators carry blood superficial → deep; valve incompetence → varicose veins

**Arches of foot**: medial longitudinal (keystone head of talus; spring ligament, tibialis posterior); lateral longitudinal (keystone cuboid; long & short plantar ligaments, peroneus longus); transverse (peroneus longus + tibialis posterior 'stirrup')

**Ischioanal fossa**: contains pudendal (Alcock's) canal with internal pudendal vessels and pudendal nerve, inferior rectal vessels/nerves, fat; communicates with opposite side behind the anal canal → horseshoe abscess
**Pelvic diaphragm**: levator ani (pubococcygeus incl. puborectalis, iliococcygeus) + coccygeus; supplied by nerve to levator ani (S4) and pudendal branches

**Pudendal nerve (S2–S4)**: leaves pelvis via greater sciatic foramen, hooks round ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, enters perineum via lesser sciatic foramen → ischial spine is the landmark for pudendal block

**Lymphatics**: testis → para-aortic (L1–L2); scrotum, vulva, lower vagina, anal canal below pectinate line → superficial inguinal; glans penis/clitoris → deep inguinal; cervix → internal & external iliac, obturator, sacral; ovary → para-aortic; uterine fundus → para-aortic (+ some via round ligament to superficial inguinal); prostate → internal iliac

points: **Coronary dominance** = artery giving the posterior descending (interventricular) artery; right-dominant in most people. LAD is the most commonly occluded vessel

**Mediastinum**: superior (above sternal angle T4/5) — thymus, arch, great veins, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct; middle — heart, pericardium, phrenic nerves; posterior — descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos, vagus, sympathetic chain. Anterior masses = 4 Ts (thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, 'terrible' lymphoma)

**Portocaval anastomoses**: lower oesophagus (left gastric ↔ azygos → varices), anorectal (superior ↔ middle/inferior rectal → rectal varices), periumbilical (paraumbilical ↔ epigastric → caput medusae), retroperitoneal (Retzius), bare area of liver

**Epiploic foramen (Winslow)**: anterior — free edge of lesser omentum with portal triad (CBD right, hepatic artery left, portal vein posterior); posterior — IVC; superior — caudate lobe; inferior — 1st part duodenum. Pringle manoeuvre clamps this edge. Morison's (hepatorenal) pouch = most dependent supine

**Gut rotation**: physiological herniation of midgut ~6th week, 270° anticlockwise rotation around SMA, return by ~10th week. Malrotation → Ladd bands, midgut volvulus (bilious vomiting in neonate). Omphalocele = covered sac, associated anomalies; gastroschisis = no sac, right of umbilicus

**Germ layers**: surface ectoderm → epidermis, lens, anterior pituitary (Rathke), enamel; neuroectoderm → CNS, retina, posterior pituitary; mesoderm → muscle, bone, heart, kidney, gonads, adrenal cortex, spleen; endoderm → GI/respiratory epithelium, liver, pancreas, thyroid follicles, parathyroid, thymus epithelium

**Development anomalies**: neural crest failure in conotruncal septation → TOF, TGA, persistent truncus; ostium secundum = commonest ASD. Kidney: ureteric bud → ureter, pelvis, calyces, collecting ducts; metanephric blastema → nephron (glomerulus to DCT); horseshoe kidney trapped under IMA

**Epithelia**: simple squamous (alveoli, endothelium), simple cuboidal (thyroid follicles, renal tubules), simple columnar (stomach, intestine), pseudostratified ciliated columnar (trachea), stratified squamous non-keratinised (oesophagus, vagina, cornea), transitional (urothelium), stratified cuboidal (sweat gland ducts)

points: **Wiggers order**: atrial systole (a wave, S4) → isovolumetric contraction (mitral closes = S1; c wave) → rapid ejection (peak aortic & LV pressure) → reduced ejection → isovolumetric relaxation (aortic closes = S2, dicrotic notch) → rapid filling (S3) → diastasis (longest phase, shortens first with tachycardia)

**JVP**: a = atrial contraction (giant: TS, pulmonary hypertension; cannon: AV dissociation/complete heart block; absent in AF); c = tricuspid bulge; x = atrial relaxation; v = atrial filling (giant cv in TR); y = tricuspid opening

**S2 splitting**: physiological on inspiration; wide variable — RBBB, pulmonary stenosis; wide fixed — ASD; reversed — LBBB, severe AS, HCM. S3 = rapid filling of volume-overloaded ventricle; S4 = atrial kick into stiff ventricle (never in AF)
**Frank–Starling**: ↑ EDV → ↑ stroke volume (optimal actin–myosin overlap + ↑ troponin C Ca²⁺ sensitivity); heterometric regulation. Positive inotropes shift the curve up/left
**Cardiac output** = HR × SV; Fick: CO = O₂ consumption ÷ (arterial − mixed venous O₂ content); MAP = CO × TPR

**Baroreflex**: carotid sinus (IX, Hering nerve) and aortic arch (X) sense stretch → NTS → ↑BP ↑firing → ↑vagal, ↓sympathetic tone; carotid sinus massage slows HR; haemorrhage ↓firing → tachycardia, vasoconstriction
**Poiseuille**: flow = ΔP·π·r⁴ / (8·η·L); resistance ∝ 1/r⁴ → halving radius raises resistance 16×; arterioles are the main resistance vessels
Coronary flow to the LV occurs mainly in diastole (compressed in systole) → tachycardia reduces LV perfusion time

traps.trap: EDV falls and SV falls because the loop 'shrinks'
traps.fix: ESV falls (ventricle empties further against lower pressure) → stroke volume and EF rise; loop gets shorter and extends to the left

traps.trap: Fast Na⁺ influx — true for ventricular and Purkinje cells
traps.fix: L-type Ca²⁺ influx. SA/AV nodal cells lack functional fast Na⁺ channels at their depolarised resting potential

traps.fix: Ostium secundum ASD: left-to-right shunt equalises respiratory changes in RV filling → wide FIXED split

points: **Body plethysmography** measures all gas incl. trapped air; helium dilution measures only communicating gas → underestimates FRC in emphysema/bullae
**V/Q**: apex ≈ 3.3 (high PAO₂, low PACO₂ — reactivation TB), base ≈ 0.6; overall ≈ 0.8. Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base, perfusion more so
**Dead space**: anatomical ≈ 150 mL (Fowler method); physiological by Bohr equation VD/VT = (PaCO₂ − PECO₂)/PaCO₂

**Compliance** ↓ in fibrosis, oedema, ARDS, surfactant deficiency; ↑ in emphysema and old age. **Surfactant** (DPPC, type II pneumocytes) lowers surface tension more in small alveoli (Laplace P = 2T/r); L:S ratio ≥ 2 = lung maturity
**Bohr effect**: CO₂/H⁺ lower Hb O₂ affinity (unloading at tissues). **Haldane effect**: oxygenation lowers Hb affinity for CO₂/H⁺ (CO₂ unloading in lungs). Normal P50 ≈ 27 mmHg
**CO poisoning**: Hb affinity ≈ 200–250× O₂; ↓ O₂ content + LEFT shift; PaO₂ and SpO₂ (pulse oximeter) normal; diagnose by CO-oximetry (COHb); 100% O₂, hyperbaric O₂ for severe cases/pregnancy

**High altitude**: hypoxia → carotid body → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis → renal HCO₃⁻ loss (acetazolamide speeds this); ↑2,3-BPG, ↑EPO → polycythaemia; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension, HAPE
**Control**: rhythm from pre-Bötzinger complex (medulla); pneumotaxic centre (upper pons) limits inspiration; apneustic (lower pons). Peripheral chemoreceptors respond strongly when PaO₂ < ~60 mmHg

**Flow–volume loops**: obstructive — scooped (concave) expiratory limb at high volumes; restrictive — small, narrow loop at low volumes with preserved/↑ FEV1/FVC; fixed upper-airway obstruction — both limbs flattened; variable extrathoracic — inspiratory flattening; variable intrathoracic — expiratory flattening

traps.stem: Fire victim, headache, SpO₂ 99% on pulse oximeter, PaO₂ 100 mmHg. Is tissue oxygenation adequate?
traps.trap: Yes — both PaO₂ and SpO₂ are normal
traps.fix: No: CO lowers O₂ content and left-shifts the curve while PaO₂ is normal; standard oximeters read COHb as oxyHb. Measure COHb by CO-oximetry and give 100% O₂

traps.stem: Primary stimulus for central chemoreceptors?
traps.trap: Arterial hypoxia or arterial H⁺ directly
traps.fix: ↑ H⁺ in CSF/brain ECF formed from CO₂ that crosses the blood–brain barrier. Hypoxia acts only via peripheral chemoreceptors

traps.stem: Best method to measure FRC in a patient with bullous emphysema?
traps.trap: Helium dilution (classic textbook method) or spirometry
traps.fix: Body plethysmography — helium does not enter non-communicating bullae and underestimates FRC; spirometry cannot measure RV/FRC at all

points: **Clearance** C = (U × V)/P. Creatinine is slightly secreted → creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR. Glucose clearance is 0 below the renal threshold (~180–200 mg/dL)
**GFR** = Kf × [(PGC − PBS) − (πGC − πBS)] ≈ 125 mL/min (180 L/day); RPF ≈ 625 mL/min; RBF = RPF ÷ (1 − Hct)
**Autoregulation** (MAP ~80–180 mmHg): myogenic afferent response + tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa senses ↑ NaCl → adenosine → afferent constriction)

**Counter-current multiplier** = loop of Henle (active NaCl out of TAL + water-permeable descending limb) builds medullary gradient up to ~1200 mOsm/kg; **counter-current exchanger** = vasa recta (passive) preserves it; urea recycling (ADH-dependent UT-A1, inner medullary CD) adds to the gradient
Fluid leaving the TAL/early DCT is always hypotonic (~100 mOsm/kg) — the diluting segment — regardless of ADH

**RAAS**: renin from JG (granular) cells of afferent arteriole — stimulated by ↓ perfusion pressure, ↓ NaCl at macula densa, β1 sympathetic; ACE mainly in pulmonary endothelium; Ang II → efferent constriction, aldosterone, ADH, thirst, PCT Na⁺ reabsorption

**Buffers**: bicarbonate = main ECF buffer (pKa 6.1 but open system); haemoglobin = main RBC/CO₂-transport buffer; phosphate = main titratable acid in urine; ammonia/NH₄⁺ = major route of renal acid excretion, ↑ in chronic acidosis. pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻ / (0.03 × PCO₂)]

**Diuretic metabolic effects**: loop & thiazide → hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis; thiazide → hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia, hypercalcaemia; loop → hypocalcaemia, ototoxicity; acetazolamide → hyperchloraemic (normal AG) metabolic acidosis; K⁺-sparing → hyperkalaemia

traps.stem: Where is most filtered water reabsorbed?
traps.trap: Collecting duct, because ADH acts there
traps.fix: PCT (~2/3, obligatory, iso-osmotic). Collecting duct handles the regulated fraction (facultative reabsorption)

traps.trap: 600 mL/min — equating PAH clearance with blood flow
traps.fix: PAH clearance ≈ RPF; RBF = 600 ÷ (1 − 0.4) = 1000 mL/min

cards.back: V2 receptor → Gs → cAMP → PKA → insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane.

cards.text: The counter-current {{c1::multiplier}} is the loop of Henle; the counter-current {{c2::exchanger}} is the vasa recta.

cards.front: Most important buffer of the ECF?
cards.back: Bicarbonate–CO₂ system (open system: CO₂ removed by lungs, HCO₃⁻ regulated by kidney).

algorithm:
Countercurrent mechanism — follow the nephron
→ Proximal tubule: reabsorbs ~65% of filtrate isotonically (Na⁺/H⁺, SGLT2 for glucose)
→ Descending limb of loop: water-permeable (aquaporin-1), impermeable to solute → filtrate becomes concentrated (up to 1200 mOsm)
→ Thick ascending limb: water-impermeable, NKCC2 pumps Na⁺ K⁺ 2Cl⁻ out → filtrate dilute (blocked by loop diuretics, interstitium loses gradient)
→ Distal tubule: NCC (thiazides block); late DT and collecting duct: ENaC (amiloride, aldosterone), aquaporin-2 inserted under ADH (V2 via Gs) → water absorbed
→ Vasa recta = countercurrent exchanger: preserves medullary gradient; urea recycling adds to the gradient
→ Result: ADH present → concentrated urine; absent (diabetes insipidus) → dilute urine

points: **Action potential**: voltage-gated Na⁺ activation → depolarisation; Na⁺ inactivation + delayed-rectifier K⁺ efflux → repolarisation; slow K⁺ closure → after-hyperpolarisation. RMP lies near E_K; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase exports 3 Na⁺, imports 2 K⁺. Absolute refractory period = Na⁺ channel inactivation

**Synapse/NMJ**: voltage-gated Ca²⁺ entry triggers exocytosis via SNAREs (botulinum cleaves SNAP-25/syntaxin/synaptobrevin; tetanus cleaves synaptobrevin). Lambert–Eaton = anti-presynaptic P/Q Ca²⁺ channel; myasthenia = anti-postsynaptic AChR

**Excitation–contraction**: skeletal — T-tubule DHP receptor (voltage sensor) mechanically opens RyR1 (malignant hyperthermia gene); cardiac — Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release via RyR2; smooth muscle — Ca²⁺–calmodulin → MLCK. Relaxation via SERCA
**Sliding filament**: A band constant; I band and H zone shorten. Length–tension: maximal active tension at optimal sarcomere length (~2.0–2.2 µm, maximum cross-bridge overlap)

**Sleep EEG**: awake relaxed eyes closed — alpha (8–13 Hz, occipital); alert — beta; N1 — theta; N2 — sleep spindles + K complexes (largest share of sleep); N3 — delta (night terrors, sleepwalking, enuresis); REM — low-voltage sawtooth waves, atonia, dreams; REM latency ↓ in depression and narcolepsy
**Hearing**: base of cochlea = high frequency, apex = low; outer hair cells (prestin) amplify and generate otoacoustic emissions; inner hair cells carry most afferent signal
**Taste**: sweet, bitter, umami via GPCR (gustducin); salty via ENaC; sour via H⁺ channels. **Smell**: GPCR (G_olf) → cAMP; only sense not relayed through the thalamus before cortex

**GI hormones**: gastrin (G cells, antrum; ↑ acid; inhibited by low pH/somatostatin); CCK (I cells; fat/amino acids → gallbladder contraction, pancreatic enzymes, Oddi relaxation); secretin (S cells; acid → pancreatic HCO₃⁻); GIP (K cells; glucose → insulin); motilin (M cells; fasting migrating motor complex; erythromycin agonist); somatostatin (D cells; universal inhibitor); VIP (VIPoma → watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria)

points: **CPS-I** is the rate-limiting urea-cycle enzyme (mitochondrial) and needs N-acetylglutamate as allosteric activator
**Acute hyperammonaemia**: stop protein, IV glucose, sodium benzoate + sodium phenylacetate/phenylbutyrate, arginine; haemodialysis if very high or refractory

algorithm:
Glycogen storage disease: pick by enzyme + clinical hallmark
→ Fasting hypoglycaemia + hepatomegaly + lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia → Type I Von Gierke: glucose-6-phosphatase
→ Cardiomegaly, hypotonia, early death in infancy → Type II Pompe: lysosomal acid α-glucosidase (enzyme replacement alglucosidase alfa)
→ Hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, limit dextrin accumulation → Type III Cori / Forbes: debranching enzyme
→ Cirrhosis, death by 5 years → Type IV Andersen: branching enzyme (abnormal glycogen long chains)
→ Exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria, no lactate rise (flat curve) → Type V McArdle: muscle glycogen phosphorylase
→ Mild liver disease → Type VI Hers: liver phosphorylase
→ Muscle phosphofructokinase-1 deficiency + haemolysis → Type VII Tarui
Lysosomal storage: Gaucher (glucocerebrosidase, crumpled-paper macrophages) · Niemann-Pick (sphingomyelinase, foamy cells + cherry red spot) · Tay-Sachs (hexosaminidase A, no hepatosplenomegaly) · Fabry (α-galactosidase A, X-linked, acroparaesthesia)

points: **Familial hypercholesterolaemia**: LDL-receptor mutation, autosomal dominant (gene dosage); homozygotes can have MI in childhood/adolescence — statin + ezetimibe ± PCSK9 inhibitor, LDL apheresis

**Ketone bodies**: acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate (dominant in DKA; NOT detected by nitroprusside dipstick), acetone. Made in liver mitochondria; liver cannot use them (lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA-transferase/thiophorase); RBCs cannot use them (no mitochondria)
**Km** = substrate concentration at ½ Vmax; low Km = high affinity. Lineweaver–Burk: y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km

Competitive inhibition is overcome by more substrate (ethanol/fomepizole vs methanol at alcohol dehydrogenase; statins at HMG-CoA reductase). Irreversible: aspirin (COX acetylation), organophosphates (AChE)
**Insulin** dephosphorylates key enzymes (activates glycogen synthase, PFK-2 kinase → ↑F-2,6-BP → glycolysis); **glucagon** phosphorylates via cAMP–PKA

**Haem synthesis**: ALA synthase (mitochondria) → ALA dehydratase (cytosol; lead-sensitive) → PBG deaminase → uroporphyrinogen III synthase → uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase → … → ferrochelatase (mitochondria; lead-sensitive)

**AIP**: PBG deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase), AD; ↑ ALA + PBG, port-wine urine darkening on standing; triggers: barbiturates, sulfonamides, alcohol, fasting, progesterone/OCP; treat haemin + IV glucose
**PCT**: uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase — commonest porphyria; blistering photosensitivity, hypertrichosis; HCV, alcohol, iron, oestrogens; treat phlebotomy or low-dose hydroxychloroquine

**Lead**: inhibits ALA dehydratase + ferrochelatase → ↑ ALA, ↑ zinc protoporphyrin, microcytic anaemia, basophilic stippling, ringed sideroblasts. Erythropoietic protoporphyria = ferrochelatase (painful non-blistering photosensitivity)

traps.stem: Young woman with recurrent abdominal pain, confusion, hyponatraemia after starting a barbiturate; skin normal.
traps.trap: Porphyria cutanea tarda — the most common porphyria
traps.fix: Acute intermittent porphyria (PBG deaminase): neurovisceral attacks without photosensitivity; ↑ urinary PBG. Treat with haemin + glucose, stop the drug

traps.stem: Adding a competitive inhibitor changes which kinetic constant?
traps.trap: Vmax falls
traps.fix: Apparent Km rises; Vmax is unchanged because enough substrate outcompetes the inhibitor

traps.stem: DKA patient improving on insulin, but urine ketone dipstick becomes MORE positive. Why?
traps.trap: Worsening ketosis — insulin failing
traps.fix: β-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate (which nitroprusside detects) as redox state improves; monitor serum β-OHB instead

points: **DNA repair**: base excision (glycosylase; MUTYH polyposis), nucleotide excision (XP — UV sensitivity, skin cancers), mismatch (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 — Lynch, microsatellite instability), homologous recombination (BRCA1/2, Fanconi, Bloom), non-homologous end joining (Artemis SCID; ATM usually tabulated here)

**Replication**: helicase unwinds, primase lays RNA primer, DNA polymerase extends only 5′→3′ (leading continuous, lagging Okazaki fragments joined by ligase); telomerase = reverse transcriptase with RNA template, active in germ/stem/cancer cells
**Topoisomerase drugs**: fluoroquinolones (bacterial gyrase/topo IV), etoposide (topo II), irinotecan/topotecan (topo I)

**CRISPR–Cas9**: guide RNA directs Cas9 to a target beside a PAM (NGG) → double-strand break → NHEJ (knockout) or HDR (precise edit). First approved CRISPR therapy (exa-cel) edits the BCL11A erythroid enhancer → ↑ HbF in sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia
**Restriction endonucleases**: bacterial enzymes cutting palindromic sites (sticky or blunt ends); basis of RFLP and cloning. Vectors by insert size: plasmid < phage λ < cosmid < BAC < YAC
**Recombinant DNA**: cut with same restriction enzyme → ligate into vector → transform host → select; first recombinant therapeutic = human insulin

**Epigenetics**: CpG-island cytosine methylation silences genes; histone acetylation (HAT) opens chromatin, deacetylation (HDAC) silences; imprinting — Prader–Willi (paternal 15q11–13 loss / maternal UPD) vs Angelman (maternal UBE3A loss / paternal UPD); azacitidine/decitabine = hypomethylating agents

traps.stem: Child with extreme photosensitivity, freckling and early skin cancers — defective repair pathway?
traps.trap: Mismatch repair (cancer predisposition) or base excision
traps.fix: Nucleotide excision repair (cannot remove UV-induced pyrimidine/thymine dimers) — xeroderma pigmentosum

traps.stem: Why does a dideoxynucleotide stop DNA synthesis in Sanger sequencing?
traps.trap: It lacks the 2′-OH group
traps.fix: It lacks the 3′-OH needed to form the next phosphodiester bond (all DNA nucleotides already lack 2′-OH)

algorithm:
Which lab technique? Ask what is being detected
→ DNA → Southern blot (DNA probe) — gene deletion, rearrangement
→ RNA → Northern blot — gene expression
→ Protein → Western blot (antibody) — HIV confirmation, prion
→ DNA-binding protein → South-western blot
→ Amplify DNA? → PCR (denature 94–95 °C, anneal 50–65 °C, extend 72 °C with Taq)
  Starting from RNA → RT-PCR (reverse transcriptase makes cDNA first)
  Quantify during run → real-time / qPCR (Ct value: lower Ct = more template)
  Mutation screening in tumour → allele-specific PCR / sequencing (Sanger = chain terminator ddNTP; NGS for many genes)
→ Cut DNA → restriction endonuclease (palindromic sites); CRISPR-Cas9 → guide RNA + Cas9 nuclease cuts at PAM-adjacent target
→ Protein/antigen detection with enzyme label → ELISA; cell surface markers → flow cytometry

points: **Best marker of vitamin D status**: serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Granulomas (sarcoidosis, TB) have extrarenal 1α-hydroxylase → hypercalcaemia
Folic acid can correct the anaemia of B12 deficiency but NOT the neurological damage → check B12 before giving folate
Thiamine before glucose in alcoholics to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy

**Zinc**: acrodermatitis enteropathica (SLC39A4/ZIP4 transporter, AR); deficiency → dysgeusia, poor wound healing, hypogonadism, growth failure. Zn enzymes: carbonic anhydrase, alcohol DH, ALA dehydratase, Cu/Zn-SOD. Childhood diarrhoea: zinc for 14 days (10 mg/day < 6 months, 20 mg/day ≥ 6 months)

**Wilson**: ATP7B → ↓ biliary copper excretion and ↓ incorporation into ceruloplasmin → ↓ serum ceruloplasmin, ↑ 24-h urinary copper, KF ring, hepatitis/cirrhosis, basal ganglia; treat penicillamine/trientine + zinc
**Menkes**: ATP7A → copper trapped in enterocytes → low serum Cu and ceruloplasmin; kinky (steely) hair, neurodegeneration, ↓ lysyl oxidase → arterial tortuosity, bladder diverticula

**Iron**: Fe²⁺ absorbed in duodenum via DMT1 (after duodenal cytochrome b reduces Fe³⁺); exported by ferroportin + hephaestin; carried by transferrin; stored as ferritin. **Hepcidin** (liver) degrades ferroportin → ↑ in inflammation (IL-6, anaemia of chronic disease), ↓ in hereditary haemochromatosis
**Selenium**: glutathione peroxidase, iodothyronine deiodinases; deficiency → Keshan cardiomyopathy, Kashin–Beck osteoarthropathy
**Iodine**: adult requirement 150 µg/day (↑ in pregnancy/lactation); deficiency → goitre, cretinism. India salt iodisation: ≥ 30 ppm at production, ≥ 15 ppm at consumer level
Molybdenum: xanthine oxidase, sulfite oxidase; fluoride < 0.5 ppm → caries, > 1.5 ppm → dental fluorosis
